messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun Mehta had been the overnight floor supervisor at a downtown Marriott for twelve years when the incident on the grand staircase shattered his routine. He was stripping the marble lobby, rushing to finish before the morning conference check-in, convinced his regional manager was watching from the mezzanine. In his hurry to buff a stubborn stain near the top step, he applied an industrial degreaser too heavily. When he turned to load the wax machine, an elderly businessman stepped onto the freshly treated patch. Arjun heard the sickening crack and the man’s sharp cry. By the time Arjun dropped his buffer and scrambled down, the man’s leg was already twisted at an unnatural angle, blood soaking through his trousers. The paramedics called it a severe comminuted fracture. Arjun called it his fault. He had been reckless. He had prioritized speed over safety. He had broken the unspoken rule of his faith and his culture: to provide and protect, not to cause harm. In the weeks that followed, Arjun’s shifts became a minefield. The polished lobby floor no longer gleamed; it glared. Sometimes, while folding linen carts in the staff laundry room, a sudden draft would stir the chemical scent of industrial degreaser, and without any gradual build-up, the lobby would flash in his mind as a series of frozen frames: the gleaming marble, the man’s falling body, the shattered hip. Each snapshot was accompanied by a heat that crawled up his neck and tightened into a hot, impotent rage. He didn’t know how to stop it. A spilled mop bucket or the squeak of a housekeeping cart could instantly summon the memory, leaving him gripping a supply cart until his knuckles whitened. These sudden intrusions soon bled into his core beliefs. He had come to believe that every time the memory struck, it pulled him downward into a certainty that he was fundamentally broken. What frightened him most was how quickly the flash cemented his conviction that he had violated the very values he had spent a lifetime upholding. The self-reproach was absolute; he told himself the injury happened solely because of his own negligence, his own inability to stay present. As the flashes repeated, the conviction deepened until the world outside his shift felt utterly hollow. He could not see purpose in his routine, nor in the empty house he returned to after his divorce. The memories did not just recall the past; they directly forged his belief that he was irredeemable and that nothing in his life held any meaning. Over months, the link between the flashes and his self-condemnation only hardened. He began arriving hours early, staying late, and avoiding the ground floor entirely. He requested transfers to the upper floors, then eventually to the back-loading docks, where the concrete was always damp and the chemical smells were masked by diesel. His supervisor noted his growing isolation and the way he flinched at the sound of rolling carts. Every time the memory intruded, the self-blame followed with immediate force, leaving him convinced that his values were shattered and his life devoid of meaning. This certainty deepened his isolation. He avoided colleagues and his ex-wife, telling himself that anyone who knew what he did would see him as a danger. Last month, while refilling a supply closet on the forty-second floor, the sharp hiss of a pressurized steam cleaner triggered the full sensory recall. Arjun dropped a box of cleaning supplies and sank to his knees, his breath catching in a panic attack. He was finally referred to occupational health. Now, sitting in the counselor’s office, Arjun is terrified of being fired and dragged back to the lobby. What he hopes for, though quietly, is to find a way to carry the weight without it crushing him, to stop the rage from dictating his mornings, and to believe, even for a moment, that he might deserve to keep going.
